To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
primary prevention of cancer is feasible and that the scientific basis for its evaluation is available.
the incidence of cancer in the study population is lower than that in the control population.

the incidence of cancer is increasing, that this increase is due to an increased prevalence of risk factors for the disease, that these risk factors are modifiable by primary prevention interventions and that such interventions are cost-effective and should therefore be given high priority.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of primary prevention programmes against cancers, based on current knowledge of the causes of cancer and of the effectiveness of interventions.

the evaluation of primary prevention programmes against the major causes of cancer, and the results of these studies should help in the formulation of national and international policies for cancer prevention.

the development of new methods for assessing the effectiveness of primary prevention programmes in reducing cancer risk, and with the application of these methods in the evaluation of existing programmes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evaluation of cancer primary prevention is a complex and difficult undertaking, which requires the use of a broad range of research methods.

primary prevention of cancer can be evaluated by means of a wide spectrum of scientific methods and approaches, but that the most important and most effective ones are those based on controlled intervention studies.
, although primary prevention of cancer is an attractive and potentially important strategy, it will require a considerable amount of scientific research before its potential can be realized.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the scientific evaluation of primary prevention programmes against cancers is a major scientific, technical and logistic undertaking, but that it is essential if we are to make the best possible use of our limited resources.
we have to be more careful about the evaluation of primary prevention programmes than about the evaluation of treatment programmes.
we are not yet able to evaluate the effectiveness of primary prevention programmes against most cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the design of primary prevention programmes against human cancer should be based on a thorough knowledge of the aetiology of the disease, and that the evaluation of such programmes should follow the same principles as those used in evaluating other public health interventions.
the evaluation of primary prevention programmes against chronic diseases is possible and necessary, but requires a great deal of planning and resources.

, in the absence of a clear understanding of the aetiological mechanisms involved in the development of the disease, it may be difficult to design an intervention that is sufficiently effective and cost-efficient to be recommended for general use.
